title: Mary McKay and the May Company record department
summary: Mary McKay, who ran the May Company jazz record department, inspired Nellie to collect records, including 12-inch 78s.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: He lived here, and I knew Tatum. I knew his wife, Ruby, and I knew her mother, and I just got to be very close to them, you know. And this Mary that we're talking about, you know, she just idolized -- well, she idolized anybody that could play anything. God knows, I don't think there's another person in this world that loved musicians, and still does, more than she did at that time. Anybody.
Let's say who Mary is.
Huh?
Let's say who Mary is.
Well, Mary is Mary Wilkerson or Mary McKay.
McKay's her married name.
Yeah, Mary McKay, that we mentioned earlier.
And I believe she used to manage the downtown May Company's record department, right?
She did. She started me collecting

records. I don't know if I even said that before, but if not I must say it now, because I credit her with really inspiring me to collect. You know, when I'd go to her house and she'd invite us to her home, and she would have just walls, just like your records are there. That was an idea that she had, only she had hers about four feet tall, Pat, all around the room. She had just like in a record shop. Like here, just like where your books are, that was nothing but records and albums. And she started me, she inspired me to collect records, you know.

Well, I've talked to a lot of people who she inspired, and they say that when she was managing that May Company department store record department, it stocked all the good jazz there was, and it was the best place in town to go buy jazz was at the May Company. Now try and find jazz in the May Company.
Right, oh, yeah.
Apparently she really -- I didn't know her then, but --

Well, she is just -- she is one woman that I wished -- of course her health isn't too good today. She's still alive, as we said before, and she's one woman that I certainly wish, you know, you could get an interview on. I don't know just how she would stand up under this, but this woman was so very instrumental in helping many musicians,

inspiring many people, because you'd sit and she'd just put records on, records, records, records, album after album, and almost anybody that you'd mention she'd have an album of them, you know. And by her being in this position -- what started -- I told her one day, I said, "Listen, Mary, I want some records. Now, when these new records come in --," she'd have something that I'd like particularly, you know. I said, "Now, I want that album," or that record, or whatever it was. She says, "Well, if I don't have it now I'll order it for you." And then she would do this, you know. I even have some of those great big discs, you know, they were 78s. Do you have any of those?
Oh, sure, sure.
The great big ones.
Well, I have 12 inch 78s.
That's what I'm talking about, the 78s.
Uh-huh, yeah, sure.

Well, they used to stock those, you know. She used to stock those records. Coleman Hawkins, "The Man I Love," and all those things. Well, I have all those things. And Mary is responsible for me having them. And I said, "Look, just call me when you get them and I'll come down and pick them up." You know? So that's how I started collecting. So I have a pretty nice record collection of my own, and I hate to have to say this, but I have not been collecting anything lately, because the things that's been happening lately
hasn't been -- hasn't really meant that much to me, you know?
